source.title: A Stochastic--Geometric Theory of Scaling Laws in Grokking
source.authors: Róisín Luo; Christian Gagné; Jonas Ngnawé; Ihsan Ullah; K. Morrissey

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or cutoff; the text includes the paper and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Tests delayed generalization on algorithmic tasks using first-hitting times and manifold-radius measurements rather than the original study’s exact method and measures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own memorization-to-generalization transition times on S5 and Z127 and their dependence on learning rate, batch size, and regularization. It does not report numerical training/test accuracy trajectories or vary training-set size. The initialization-radius analysis and cited results from prior work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains MLPs on S5 and Z127 and measures first-hitting times of the memorization (train-loss) and generalization (true-loss) boundaries. Generalization arrives about 7–13× later than memorization, which bears directly on V1's delayed-generalization claim. It uses loss-boundary hitting times rather than accuracy curves.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors conclude that Adam with coupled ℓ2 regularization induces a shell–core geometry: an initialization shell encloses a memorization shell, which encloses a generalization core. Grokking is the stochastic first-passage from memorization to generalization. Stopping-time analysis yields scaling laws for the radii and the transition time in η, b and λ, validated on S5 and Z127 and said to recover the τ ∝ 1/(ηλ) scaling reported in prior work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses structured algorithmic tasks and Adam with ℓ2 regularization, but analyzes first-hitting times and parameter-space radii rather than directly reporting the original study’s training/test accuracy curves or training-set-size effect.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports transition-time and manifold-radius sweeps over learning rate, batch size, and ℓ2 regularization coefficient. It also states that 16-bit precision can introduce numerical instability in grokking; no corresponding controlled transition-time result is reported.

fits_no_version.finding: The memorization-to-generalization delay scales with learning rate, batch size and ℓ2 coefficient on S5 and Z127 (Figures 5 and 13). The authors claim it recovers τ ∝ 1/(ηλ) and fit a theoretical curve.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking delay length scales inversely with ηλ and depends weakly on batch size under Adam with coupled ℓ2 regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: Parameter norm shrinks from initialization (≈248–255) to the memorization boundary (≈185) to the generalization boundary (≈70–72) (Tables 1–2, Figures 2, 4, 11, 12). Generalizing solutions lie at much smaller norm.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under weight shrinkage, generalizing solutions occupy a low-norm core inside a shell of memorizing solutions, and the delay is the time to contract radially between them.

record.problems: The text does not give explicit training/test accuracy trajectories or test the training-set-size dependence in V1. Several scaling results are shown only in figures without stated numerical values. The paper states its theory depends on a sufficiently small learning rate and sufficiently large batch size, and does not directly apply to the large-η/b regime.

untested.parts: No test-accuracy values showing a chance-to-near-perfect jump, and the abruptness of the jump is not measured. The training-set fraction is neither stated nor varied, so the claim that the delay grows as the training set shrinks is untested.
No circuit-level or continuous progress measures anticipating the jump.
No non-algorithmic data. No initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation switching grokking on or off.
No test of circuit efficiency, critical dataset size, or ungrokking. The λ sweeps measure only delay length and radii.
No comparison of learned algorithms across runs.
The authors remark that 16-bit precision can destabilize grokking, but report no controlled result. They do not show that the delay disappears under other optimizers or precision settings.

missing.what: Mean radii ρ0, ρM and ρG with their seed standard deviations (e.g. S5: 248.25, 185.53, 69.50), recording norm shrinkage across the delay.
The training-set fraction is never stated, which limits comparison of delay length with other V1 studies.

record.verdict_notes: The study is mainly theoretical. Its experiments use generalization defined as true loss below ε, with no accuracy curves, so 'near-perfect' is inferred rather than shown. Table 2's caption says S5 but the data are Z127. The theory is stated not to apply to the large-η/b regime.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report explicit chance-to-near-perfect test-accuracy values or vary training-set size to test whether smaller sets increase the delay.
No circuit-level measurement of Fourier algorithms, memorizing components, or continuous progress measures anticipating an accuracy jump.
No non-algorithmic data, initialization-scale sweep, weight-norm sweep testing a lazy-to-rich transition, or switching grokking on or off.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.

Although the paper varies the ℓ2 regularization coefficient and measures transition times, it does not test whether low norm favors a more efficient circuit over memorization, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below it.
No test of whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm.
The paper notes that 16-bit precision can introduce numerical instability in grokking, but does not test whether the delay is an optimizer/numerical artifact that disappears when controlled.

relation.reason: Its own training experiments measure the separation between memorization and generalization, although those measurements cannot establish the exact accuracy-defined V1 effect.

tranche.reason: The study directly investigates delayed generalization on algorithmic tasks through loss-boundary stopping times and stochastic-geometric analysis, a different operationalization aimed at the same question.

source_check.notes: Tables 1–2 report descriptive stopping-time summaries without separate control baselines; τM supplies an internal timing reference. Table 2 is titled Z127 but erroneously repeats S5 in its caption.

reader_labels.condition: S5 and Z127 under the reported base training configuration and the reported learning-rate, batch-size, and regularization sweeps
reader_labels.reason: Both tasks have a prolonged measured interval between memorization and generalization, and the authors state the transition-time scaling experiments validate their predictions (r1-r12).
